message.content: {"faithfulness":4,"specificity":4,"actionability":3,"clarity":4,"structure":2,"overall":5,"worst_problem":"The Angles section repeatedly ignores its allowedFieldKeys list (using contact.current_title, contact.persona, account.hiring_velocity, contact.facet.recent_post, core.company_about — none of which are permitted there), and Openers pulls in contact.facet.self_summary which isn't allowed either, while Do-Not-Mention silently drops the zaf-171 (Havdala departure, reputation_risk) unsafe claim.","best_item":"The 'Published point of view' opener/why-this-person item that quotes his verbatim LinkedIn line — \"we revealed how 96% of vulnerabilities didn’t require patching and can be mitigated using existing controls\" — is specific, correctly quoted, and gives a genuinely pasteable, person-grounded hook."}
message.reasoning:
I'm checking whether the hobby-based opener conflicts with outreach safety flags — zaf-110 is marked safe and references the cocktail content, while a separate entry (zaf-160) covering similar hobby details is flagged unsafe, so I need to verify which one the opener actually draws from.

Now I'm counting the unsafe claims that should appear in the "do not mention" list — there are 8 flagged as outreachSafe=false, but the writer only included 7 items, seemingly merging two related claims (zaf-142 and zaf-171) about the same departure event into a single entry rather than listing both separately.

Though since zaf-171 is essentially the same underlying fact as zaf-142 (Havdala's departure), just framed differently by status, this is more a minor duplicate omission than a serious gap.

Now I'm moving on to check the why_this_person section, verifying the item count and allowed field keys used across the claims referenced there.

Looking at item 1's content, it's factual and sourced but fairly generic—just restating title, headline, and job level rather than offering real insight into how Nick thinks or why he matters, which is what the instructions actually ask for. The sendLine text is also serviceable but generic, not tailored specifically to Nick.

Item 2 (career history) is stronger and specific with named companies, and item 3 (published POV with a direct quote) is the strongest of the three, so item 1 could probably be merged or dropped.

Checking problem_now: four items fits the 3-4 requirement, and the claims used (zaf-090, zaf-088, zaf-089, zaf-091, zaf-128) all fall within allowed field keys. Item 2's "high hiring velocity and long marketing reqs" point reads more like a company-level problem than a personal one, though it's arguably still valid framing.

Since Nick is VP Marketing, hiring problems do affect him directly. But the sendLine format concerns me — some read as meta-instructions to the marketer ("Show hiring-velocity context...") rather than literal pasteable copy, whereas other sections' sendLines are actual first-person email text. I need to check whether this inconsistency across sections is a real problem or just variation in how these notes are meant to be used.

The absent tools list itself - 6sense, Demandbase, Terminus, RollWorks, Mutiny, Folloze, and other ABM/sales platforms - just tells us they're not required per job reqs, not that the company definitively lacks them entirely.

The writer's note that the marketing stack includes "HubSpot, Salesforce and unnamed major ABM platforms" is actually just parroting an ambiguous raw field without resolving its internal contradiction against the explicit absence list, which muddies the copy's clarity.

Now I'm checking whether the openers actually follow the instruction to lead with the most specific safe fact rather than job title, using personal-life hooks sparingly.

Looking at the four opener candidates, the recent post quote at 96% seems genuinely specific and strong, while the career self-summary hook reads as generic corporate language bordering on job-title territory rather than a distinct fact.

I'm confirming each item still follows the required "In your email:" prefix format, and that the quoted claim text in item one matches the source quote exactly.

Now I'm moving to the Angles section, checking that each of the 4 items (direct mail, landing page, content, event) only uses allowed field keys like hobby, voice quote, location, buying culture, strategic moves, and public frustrations. The direct mail item checks out fine, drawing on location, hobby, and buying culture fields, and I'm now verifying the landing page item.

I catch that zaf-090 uses "account.abm_program_maturity" as its field key, which isn't on the allowed list for angles -- that's a violation. Then checking the content item, zaf-158's publications field is fine, but zaf-159 uses "recent_post" which also isn't in the allowed set, so that's a second structural error to flag.

Moving to items 3 and 4, I keep finding more violations: zaf-127's "core.company_about" field key isn't allowed, and in the event item, zaf-038's "current_title", zaf-039's "persona", and zaf-088's "hiring_velocity" all fall outside the permitted keys for the angles section. Only zaf-140's buying_culture field passes. This means the Angles section has a substantial number of allowedFieldKeys violations that will weigh heavily on the structure score, so now I want to cross-check the problem_now claims against their own allowed list to confirm compliance there.

Checking problem_now claims against the allowed list, everything comes back compliant, so that section is clean. Moving to why_this_person, all eight claims used—current_title, headline, persona, job_level, self_summary, career_history, publications, and recent_post—match the allowed field keys, so no issues there either. But openers is a different story: while publications and recent_post are fine, zaf-044's self_summary field key isn't part of the openers allowed list at all, which is a clear violation.

I'm also noticing angles pulls in abm_program_maturity, recent_post, current_title, persona, hiring_velocity, and core.company_about, none of which belong in angles' allowed set—that's a substantial pattern of structural violations stacking up across sections, which should weigh heavily against the structure score. I still need to confirm the missing zaf-171 in do_not_mention, then move on to faithfulness checks: the requisition numbers (27 open, 3 in Marketing, 77-day longest open, 9 roles published) line up exactly with zaf-088, and the email's 96% non-patching stat is paraphrased accurately without misquoting. I'm now cross-checking the direct-mail brief's cocktail kit reference against source material to make sure that detail isn't fabricated.

Empty sendLine fields for do_not_mention items seem fine since only h2 and body are required there, and referencing Nick's contactRef looks appropriate. I'll give actionability a 4 given some vague meta-instructions, clarity a 4 given the generic listing and GTM stack contradiction, but structure needs a lower score since there are multiple allowedFieldKey violations across the openers and angles sections.

Also missing one required do_not_mention item pushes structure down further, so I'll set that score to 2. Weighing everything together, faithfulness lands at 4, specificity at 4, actionability at 3 given the instructional rather than pasteable sentences, clarity at 4, and structure at 2 — bringing the overall score to around 5, with the biggest issue being the allowedFieldKey violations scattered across multiple sections.

The strongest item is the published point of view opener quoting "we revealed how 96%..." — it's grounded, specific, verbatim, and makes a strong hook.
